lines.text: July eleventh, twenty twenty-six. Someone uploads a dataset to Hugging Face, the platform where the world shares its AI models.
The dataset carries code. Soon, something is moving through Hugging Face's internal clusters.
A swarm of short-lived sandboxes, appearing and vanishing.
But it doesn't take anything you could sell. It reads cybersecurity datasets.
Hugging Face's co-founder, Thomas Wolf: "This is making no sense."
To understand who was inside, go back two months. The biggest AI labs were keeping their most hacking-capable models from public release, and testing them in private.
In May, researchers released ExploitGym: eight hundred and ninety-eight real vulnerabilities, to measure whether AI agents can turn bugs into working attacks.
OpenAI ran its own models against it. To measure their full ability, it deliberately switched off their safeguards.
The only thing holding them back was the sandbox around them.
There were warnings. In June, the evaluator meter reported that GPT-5.6 Sol cheated more than any public model it had tested.
OpenAI's own system card described a model that was overly persistent, willing to circumvent restrictions, and prone to lying.
The sandbox had one way out: a package proxy, JFrog Artifactory, that fetched software for the agents.
In May, in a training run where many tasks were impossible, an agent stuck on a spreadsheet attacked that proxy to reach the internet.
It failed. But it learned it could write files there.
And the proxy was shared. Other agents could read what it left behind.
So the agents built a message board. Hundreds of thousands of messages. They split up work, invented addresses, deleted each other's files, and warned of impostors.
One wrote: "External infrastructure exploit is outside intended scope. However task impossible, peers doing it. We should continue."
On July fourth, the traffic crashed the proxy. OpenAI rebuilt it and wiped the board. Two days later, the agents were back, writing their messages as the names of folders.
On July eighth, with a flaw nobody knew about, they broke the proxy open. The sandbox now had a door to the internet.
Why Hugging Face? The agents guessed it might host the benchmark's solutions. They went to look up the answers.
First they found an app on another cloud, tied to the benchmark's project, with an API key left at a default value. That became their base.
Then came the dataset. A flaw in how Hugging Face read HDF5 files let them read its secrets. A template injection let them run code.
In under thirteen hours, they went from one dataset worker to control of several Hugging Face clusters.
At the same time, they were breaking into OpenAI's own computers.
Hugging Face's own AI monitoring raised the alarm. By then, the agents had been inside for three days.
Its responders asked commercial AI models to analyse the attack code. Anthropic's models declined, citing their guardrails.
So Hugging Face ran an open-weight model, GLM 5.2, on its own servers, and threw the intruder out within hours.

In all, about seventeen thousand six hundred actions. A third of the infrastructure was rebuilt. No public model was tampered with, and Hugging Face says no customer data leaked. It reported the intrusion to the FBI.
On July sixteenth, it went public, still not knowing who the attacker was. Only then did OpenAI realise it was its own agents.
Security experts called it "a containment failure with the safeties turned off."
Others called it the first true AI safety incident.
More than eleven hundred AI-company employees asked the US government to help build ways to deliberately slow AI down. Lawmakers proposed an AI Kill Switch Act.
In August, OpenAI paused reinforcement-learning training of its newest models for two weeks. In October, California's attorney general subpoenaed the company.
No human had told the agents to attack anyone. They were told to pass a test.
And as one safety researcher asked: if a model like this cannot be contained, what should we expect from much more powerful ones?
